```{r}
#| echo: false
#| include: false

# --- Setup: generate all datasets ---
library(tidyverse)

set.seed(2026)
n <- 1000

complete_data <- tibble(
    id = 1:n,
    sex = rep(c("Male", "Female"), each = n / 2),
    height = round(
        c(
            rnorm(n / 2, mean = 175, sd = 7),
            rnorm(n / 2, mean = 162, sd = 6)
        ),
        1
    )
) |>
    mutate(
        p_complete = plogis(
            -0.11 * (height - 170)
        ),
        profile_status = ifelse(
            rbinom(n(), 1, p_complete) == 1,
            "Incomplete",
            "Complete"
        )
    ) |>
    select(-p_complete)

# Door A
set.seed(101)
data_a <- complete_data |>
    mutate(height = ifelse(runif(n()) < 0.40, NA, height))

# Door B
set.seed(102)
data_b <- complete_data |>
    mutate(
        p_miss = ifelse(profile_status == "Incomplete", 0.70, 0.05),
        height = ifelse(runif(n()) < p_miss, NA, height)
    ) |>
    select(-p_miss)

# Door C
set.seed(103)
data_c <- complete_data |>
    mutate(
        p_miss = case_when(
            sex == "Female" ~ 0.10,
            height < 170 ~ 0.60,
            height > 180 ~ 0.10,
            TRUE ~ 0.10 + (180 - height) / (180 - 170) * 0.50
        ),
        height = ifelse(runif(n()) < p_miss, NA, height)
    ) |>
    select(-p_miss)

# Door D: the complete data (no corruption)
data_d <- complete_data
```

            "Incomplete",
            "Complete"
        )
    ) |>
    select(-p_complete)

set.seed(101)
data_a <- complete_data |>
    mutate(height = ifelse(runif(n()) < 0.40, NA, height))

set.seed(102)
data_b <- complete_data |>
    mutate(
        p_miss = ifelse(profile_status == "Incomplete", 0.70, 0.05),

    ) |>
    select(-p_miss)

set.seed(103)
data_c <- complete_data |>
    mutate(
        p_miss = case_when(
            sex == "Female" ~ 0.10,

        ),
        height = ifelse(runif(n()) < p_miss, NA, height)

data_d <- complete_data

## Welcome, Players

:::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
You are **data analysts** at a dating app. Your company collected data on **1,000 users** — height, sex, and whether they completed their full profile.

But something went wrong. The data was incomplete, and now **four different versions** exist. Only one is the original.

**Your goal**: pick a door, analyze the data behind it, and figure out if your data has the truth.

:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
![](https://media.giphy.com/media/v1.Y2lkPTc5MGI3NjExNjcydndpdHZrcHNudnJ2bDhlMm1zOGM2Ym1wYzloY3gzNmNqc2tqeSZlcD12MV9naWZzX3NlYXJjaCZjdD1n/2mzPaYFmVGBITEZUNW/giphy.gif)
:::

# Round 1: Pick a Door  

## The Four Doors

:::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
![](https://media.giphy.com/media/v1.Y2lkPWVjZjA1ZTQ3cWd0cDVjbjdvbmRwMGMzejcwMjl5Ym1pb2N3bmw5OXg3MjAwa3oxZyZlcD12MV9naWZzX3NlYXJjaCZjdD1n/AXzzeV66BR4p2Z3XYf/giphy.gif):::
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
Behind each door is a version of your dating app data with the same 1,000 users. Three were corrupted by a **different unknown force**. One was left untouched.

**You must choose one door. That's your dataset.**

One door has no missing values at all, you know the truth, so please don't tell us your data is complete.

:::
::::

## Choose Your Door

Run this code to randomly select your door:

```{webr-r}
# Pick your door!
my_door <- sample(c("A", "B", "C", "D"), 1)
cat("You opened Door", my_door, "\n")

my_data <- switch(my_door,
    "A" = data_a,
    "B" = data_b,
    "C" = data_c,
    "D" = data_d
)
```

Write down which door you got. Now let's see what's behind it.

## Open Your Door

Compute the group means from your dataset:

```{webr-r}
my_data |>
    summarise(
        n_complete = sum(!is.na(height)),
        n_missing = sum(is.na(height)),
        mean_height = round(mean(height, na.rm = TRUE), 1),
        sd_height = round(sd(height, na.rm = TRUE), 1),
        .by = sex
    )
```

**Write down your results:**

-   Male mean height = ?
-   Female mean height = ?
-   How many missing values do you have?

We'll compare answers across the class in a moment.

## Look around the zoom:

-   **Did everyone get the same means?**
-   **Did anyone have zero missing values? (don't tell)**

> The force behind each door determined whether your results are trustworthy.

## All Four Doors Opened 

Let's see what was behind every door:

```{r}
#| echo: false
get_summary <- function(data, name) {
    data |>
        group_by(sex) |>
        summarise(
            mean = round(mean(height, na.rm = TRUE), 1),
            .groups = "drop"
        ) |>
        pivot_wider(names_from = sex, values_from = mean) |>
        mutate(
            Dataset = name,
            Difference = round(Male - Female, 1),
            .before = 1
        )
}

puzzle <- bind_rows(
    get_summary(data_a, "Door A"),
    get_summary(data_b, "Door B"),
    get_summary(data_c, "Door C"),
    get_summary(data_d, "Door D")
) |>
    relocate(Difference, .after = Male)

knitr::kable(
    puzzle,
    col.names = c("Door", "Female", "Male", "Difference (M <U+2212> F)")
)
```


# Round 2: The Three Forces

## Naming the Forces

Rubin [-@rubin1976inference] identified three forces that make data disappear. Each one leaves a different trace and requires a different strategy.

| Force (Full Name)                        | Missingness depends on...      |
|------------------------------------------|-------------------------------|
| **MCAR (Missing Completely At Random)**  | Nothing — purely random        |
| **MAR (Missing At Random)**              | Observed variables only        |
| **MNAR (Missing Not At Random)**         | The missing values themselves  |

Learn to recognize each one, then we'll see which force hit your door.

## Force 1: MCAR — The Random Storm

:::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
**Definition**: The probability of being missing is **unrelated** to any variable  observed or unobserved.

$$P(R = 1 \mid \text{Sex}, \text{Height}) = P(R = 1)$$

> *In plain language*: This force strikes like lightning *completely at random*. It doesn't care who you are or what your height is.
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
**Where you'll encounter it**:

-   A server crash deletes random records
-   You don't ask for height to some users (randomly)
-   People did not see the height question because it was behind a banner that appears randomly

**Good news**: Complete-case analysis is **unbiased**; you lose statistical power.
:::
::::

## Planned Missing Data Designs (MCAR by Design) {.smaller}

:::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}

Researchers sometimes intentionally introduce MCAR to reduce participant burden while preserving statistical power.

**Three-form design** [@Graham_2006]:

- All participants answer a common block (X)
- Each participant is randomly assigned two of three additional blocks (A, B, C)
- Every item pair appears together in at least one form

| Form | Blocks |
|------|--------|
| 1    | X + A + B |
| 2    | X + A + C |
| 3    | X + B + C |

:::

::: {.column width="50%"}

**Why do this?**

-   Cuts survey length by ~33% per participant
-   Reduces fatigue and careless responding
-   Missingness is **MCAR by construction** (random assignment to forms)
-   MI or FIML recovers full-data estimates with minimal efficiency loss

**Other planned designs:**

-   **Two-method measurement** - expensive gold-standard measure on a random subsample, cheap proxy for everyone
-   **Wave-missing** - in longitudinal studies, skip a random subset of participants at certain waves


:::
::::

## Force 2: MAR - The Hidden Trail

:::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
**Definition**: The probability of being missing depends on **observed** data, but **not** on the missing value itself.

$$P(R = 1 \mid Y_{\text{obs}}, Y_{\text{mis}}) = P(R = 1 \mid Y_{\text{obs}})$$

> *In plain language*: This force follows a trail you *can* see. If you find the trail, you can undo the damage.
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
**Where you'll encounter it**:

-   Users who skip their full profile also skip reporting height
-   Newer users are less likely to fill in optional fields
-   Users who never upload a photo also leave height blank

**Key**: Complete-case analysis can be **biased**, but proper methods (MI, FIML) can correct it *if* you follow the right trail.
:::
::::

## Force 3: MNAR - The Invisible Wall

:::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
**Definition**: The probability of being missing depends on the **missing value itself**, even after controlling for observed data.

$$P(R = 1 \mid \text{Sex}, \text{Height}) \newline \text{depends directly on height}$$

> *In plain language*: This is the most dangerous force. The data hides *because* of what it contains. There is no visible trail to follow.
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
**Where you'll encounter it**:

-   Shorter men don't report their height on dating apps
-   High earners refuse to report income
-   Sickest patients drop out of clinical trials

**Warning**: **No standard method** can fully correct this bias. You'll need sensitivity analysis.
:::
::::

## Your Map of the Forces {.smaller}

| Feature                  | MCAR (Random Storm) | MAR (Hidden Trail)   | MNAR (Invisible Wall) |
|--------------------------|---------------------|----------------------|-----------------------|
| **Depends on**           | Nothing             | Observed variables   | The missing values    |
| **Complete-case bias?**  | No                  | Yes                  | Yes                   |
| **Fixable with MI/FIML?**| Yes (N/A)          | Yes                  | Not fully             |
| **How common?**          | Rare                | Common               | Common                |
| **Testable?**            | Partially           | Not definitively     | Not definitively      |


::: {.callout-important}
We can never fully verify whether data is MAR or MNAR from the observed data alone. The classification requires *substantive reasoning* about the data-generating process.
:::

Now, can you match each force to one of the doors?

# Round 3: The Reveal

## How It Works

I'm going to show you the code used to generate each door's dataset.

Your job: read the code and tell me what mechanism it is.

-   Is missingness related to nothing? → *MCAR*
-   Is missingness related to an observed variable? → *MAR*
-   Is missingness related to the missing value itself? → *MNAR*

## Door A: The Code {.smaller}

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| eval: false

data_a <- complete_data |>
    mutate(
        height = ifelse(runif(n()) < 0.40, NA, height)
    )
```

**What do you see?**

-   What determines whether height goes missing?
-   Does it depend on sex? On height? On profile status?

. . .

> *MCAR — The Random Storm.* Every observation has the same 40% chance of being missing. It depends on nothing — pure random chance. The complete cases are a random subset of the data. You lose power, but the truth survives.

## Door B: The Code {.smaller}

First, how `profile_status` was generated:

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| eval: false

# Profile completion depends on height
complete_data <- complete_data |>
    mutate(
        p_complete = plogis(
            -0.11 * (height - 170)
        ),
        profile_status = ifelse(
            rbinom(n(), 1, p_complete) == 1,
            "Incomplete",
            "Complete"
        )
    )
```

Then missingness in height depends on `profile_status`:

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| eval: false

data_b <- complete_data |>
    mutate(
        p_miss = ifelse(profile_status == "Incomplete", 0.70, 0.05),
        height = ifelse(runif(n()) < p_miss, NA, height)
    )
```

**What do you see?**

-   `profile_status` depends on height; shorter users are less likely to complete their profile
-   Missingness in height depends on `profile_status`; not on height directly

. . .

> *MAR - The Hidden Trail.* Missingness depends on an observed variable (`profile_status`). Since shorter users tend to have incomplete profiles (and thus more missing height), the naive group means are biased upward. If we control for `profile_status`, we can recover the truth.

## Door B: Controlling for Profile Status

Try it yourself — estimate the mean height by sex, **controlling for profile status**:

```{webr-r}
# Step 1: subgroup means (observed) weighted by total subgroup size
data_b |>
    summarise(
        n_total = n(),
        n_observed = sum(!is.na(height)),
        mean_height = mean(height, na.rm = TRUE),
        .by = c(sex, profile_status)
    ) |>
    summarise(
        mean_height = round(weighted.mean(mean_height, w = n_total), 1),
        .by = sex
    )
```

We can also recover the marginal means using regression + `predict`:

```{webr-r}
# Fit regression controlling for profile_status
mod <- lm(height ~ sex * profile_status, data = data_b)

# Predicted marginal means by sex
data_b |>
    mutate(pred = predict(mod, newdata = data_b)) |>
    summarise(
        mean_height = round(mean(pred), 1),
        .by = sex
    )
```

## Door C: The Code {.smaller}

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| eval: false

data_c <- complete_data |>
    mutate(
        p_miss = case_when(
            sex == "Female" ~ 0.10,
            height < 170 ~ 0.60,
            height > 180 ~ 0.10,
            TRUE ~ 0.10 + (180 - height) / (180 - 170) * 0.50
        ),
        height = ifelse(runif(n()) < p_miss, NA, height)
    )
```

**What do you see?**

-   What determines whether height goes missing for males?
-   Can you observe `height` if it's the variable that went missing?

. . .

> *MNAR - The Invisible Wall.* Among males, missingness depends on height itself; the variable that's missing. Shorter males have up to 60% chance of being missing. There's no observed trail to follow.

No standard method can fully correct this.

## Door D: The Code {.smaller}

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| eval: false

data_d <- complete_data
```

. . .

> *No problem at all.* Door D is the complete, original data; no missing values, no mechanism.

```{r}
#| echo: false
truth <- complete_data |>
    group_by(sex) |>
    summarise(m = round(mean(height), 1))
```

If you chose this door, you had the truth the whole time.

> *Ground truth*: Male = `r truth$m[truth$sex == "Male"]`, Female = `r truth$m[truth$sex == "Female"]`

## The Evidence Board {.smaller}

Now let's compare all four doors against the truth:

```{r}
#| echo: false
comparison <- bind_rows(
    get_summary(data_d, "Door D (Truth)"),
    get_summary(data_a, "Door A (MCAR)"),
    get_summary(data_b, "Door B (MAR)"),
    get_summary(data_c, "Door C (MNAR)")
)

knitr::kable(
    comparison,
    col.names = c("Door", "Difference", "Female", "Male")
)
```

. . .

> *Door A* (MCAR): close to the truth; random loss, no bias

. . .

> *Door B* (MAR): biased; but fixable if we control for `profile_status`

. . .

> *Door C* (MNAR): biased; and not fixable with standard methods

## Visualizing the Damage {.smaller}

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 6
bind_rows(
    data_d |> mutate(dataset = "Door D (Truth)"),
    data_a |> filter(!is.na(height)) |> mutate(dataset = "Door A (MCAR)"),
    data_b |> filter(!is.na(height)) |> mutate(dataset = "Door B (MAR)"),
    data_c |> filter(!is.na(height)) |> mutate(dataset = "Door C (MNAR)")
) |>
    mutate(
        dataset = factor(
            dataset,
            levels = c(
                "Door D (Truth)",
                "Door A (MCAR)",
                "Door B (MAR)",
                "Door C (MNAR)"
            )
        )
    ) |>
    ggplot(aes(x = height, fill = sex)) +
    geom_density(alpha = 0.5) +
    facet_wrap(~dataset, nrow = 2) +
    scale_fill_manual(values = c("Female" = "#F47321", "Male" = "#005030")) +
    labs(x = "Height (cm)", y = "Density", fill = "Sex") +
    theme_minimal(base_size = 14) +
    theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

## MAR: Why Is It Biased? {.smaller}

`profile_status` depends on height. Shorter users are less likely to complete their profile:

```{r}
#| echo: true
complete_data |>
    summarise(
        n = n(),
        mean_height = round(mean(height), 1),
        .by = c(sex, profile_status)
    ) |>
    knitr::kable()
```

. . .

Shorter users → incomplete profile → more missing height → observed means are biased **upward**.

## MAR: Following the Trail {.smaller}

But within each profile-status group, missing and observed cases have **similar** mean heights:

```{r}
#| echo: true
complete_data |>
    mutate(status = ifelse(is.na(data_b$height), "Missing", "Observed")) |>
    summarise(
        n = n(),
        mean_height = round(mean(height), 1),
        .by = c(profile_status, status)
    ) |>
    knitr::kable()
```

. . .

This is the signature of MAR. If we include `profile_status` as an **auxiliary variable** in MI/FIML, we recover unbiased estimates.

## MNAR: Behind the Wall {.smaller}

```{r}
#| echo: true
complete_data |>
    mutate(status = ifelse(is.na(data_c$height), "Missing", "Observed")) |>
    summarise(
        n = n(),
        mean_height = round(mean(height), 1),
        .by = c(profile_status, status)
    ) |>
    knitr::kable()
```

. . .

Among males, missing cases are shorter than observed cases. The data disappears *because of its own value*. No observed variable can explain this; the bias is not fixable with standard methods.

## Mapping the Three Forces {.smaller}

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 11
#| fig-height: 4.5
library(patchwork)

p1 <- ggplot() +
    geom_hline(yintercept = 0.30, color = "#F47321", linewidth = 2) +
    annotate(
        "text",
        x = 175,
        y = 0.38,
        label = "P(Missing) = 0.30",
        size = 4.5,
        color = "#F47321",
        fontface = "bold"
    ) +
    annotate(
        "text",
        x = 175,
        y = 0.18,
        label = "Same probability for everyone",
        size = 3.5,
        color = "#666666"
    ) +
    scale_x_continuous(limits = c(145, 200)) +
    ylim(0, 1) +
    labs(
        title = "MCAR: The Random Storm",
        x = "Height (cm)",
        y = "P(Missing)"
    ) +
    theme_minimal(base_size = 11)

p2 <- tibble(
    profile = factor(
        c("Incomplete", "Complete"),
        levels = c("Incomplete", "Complete")
    ),
    p_miss = c(0.70, 0.05)
) |>
    ggplot(aes(x = profile, y = p_miss, fill = profile)) +
    geom_col(width = 0.5) +
    scale_fill_manual(
        values = c("Incomplete" = "#F47321", "Complete" = "#005030")
    ) +
    geom_text(
        aes(label = scales::percent(p_miss)),
        vjust = -0.5,
        size = 4,
        fontface = "bold"
    ) +
    ylim(0, 1) +
    labs(
        title = "MAR: The Hidden Trail",
        x = "Profile Status (observed)",
        y = "P(Missing)"
    ) +
    theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
    theme(legend.position = "none")

p3 <- tibble(height = seq(145, 200, 0.5)) |>
    crossing(sex = c("Male", "Female")) |>
    mutate(
        p_miss = case_when(
            sex == "Female" ~ 0.10,
            height < 170 ~ 0.60,
            height > 180 ~ 0.10,
            TRUE ~ 0.10 + (180 - height) / (180 - 170) * 0.50
        )
    ) |>
    ggplot(aes(x = height, y = p_miss, color = sex)) +
    geom_line(linewidth = 2) +
    scale_color_manual(values = c("Female" = "#F47321", "Male" = "#005030")) +
    ylim(0, 1) +
    labs(
        title = "MNAR: The Invisible Wall",
        x = "Height (cm) <U+2014> the missing variable",
        y = "P(Missing)",
        color = "Sex"
    ) +
    theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
    theme(legend.position = "bottom")

p1 + p2 + p3
```

## The Takeaway

:::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
**If you ignore the forces:**

-   Group means are biased
-   Treatment effects are distorted
-   Confidence intervals miss the truth
-   p-values are unreliable
-   Effect sizes are attenuated
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
**Real-world consequences:**

-   Clinical trials underestimate side effects
-   Surveys underrepresent vulnerable groups
-   Longitudinal studies suffer from survivor bias
-   Policy decisions rest on distorted evidence
:::
::::

. . .

> *The method for handling missing data should be informed by the mechanism that generated it.* Rubin

## Apply to Your Own Research

Consider your own research or a study you've recently read:

1.  Which variables might have missing data?
2.  What force (*MCAR*, *MAR*, *MNAR*) is most plausible? Why?
3.  What would happen if you just deleted all incomplete cases?
4.  What observed variables might predict the missingness?

## Lessons Learned

1.  **Missing data mechanisms matter**. They determine whether your results are biased
2.  **MCAR** (the random storm) is the only safe scenario for complete-case analysis and it's the rarest
3.  **MAR** (the hidden trail) can be addressed with proper methods if you follow the right auxiliary variables
4.  **MNAR** (the invisible wall) is the hardest challenge requires substantive reasoning and sensitivity analysis
5.  **Always ask why data is missing**, not just how much

# Part II: The Toolkit

## Equipping Yourself

Now that you can name the forces, you need the right tools to deal with them.

-   Complete-case analysis: Deleting incomplete cases
-   Multiple Imputation (MI): Creating plausible completed datasets
-   Full Information Maximum Likelihood (FIML): Using all available information
-   Sensitivity analysis: What to do when you suspect MNAR

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| include: false

# --- Part II Setup: Multiple Imputation with MICE ---
library(mice)

set.seed(752)
n_mi <- 250

mi_complete <- tibble(
    id = 1:n_mi,
    age = round(rnorm(n_mi, mean = 0, sd = 1), 2),
    female = rbinom(n_mi, 1, 0.55),
    treatment = rbinom(n_mi, 1, 0.5),
    baseline_severity = round(rnorm(n_mi, mean = 0, sd = 1), 2),
    social_support = round(rnorm(n_mi, mean = 0, sd = 1), 2),
    stress = round(rnorm(n_mi, mean = 0, sd = 1), 2),
    outcome = round(
        -0.5 * treatment - 0.3 * age + 0.4 * female +
            0.5 * baseline_severity - 0.3 * social_support +
            0.8 * stress + rnorm(n_mi, 0, 1), 2
    )
)

# MAR missingness <U+2014> strong differential dropout to expose complete-case bias.
# stress is an auxiliary variable: it affects outcome and drives dropout,
# but is NOT included in the analysis model.
# P(outcome missing) depends on stress AND treatment (both fully observed).
# P(social_support missing) depends on age (observed).
# Complete-case is biased because high-stress treated patients are dropped,
# distorting the treatment-outcome relationship.
# MI recovers because stress is in the imputation model.
mi_data <- mi_complete |>
    mutate(
        p_miss_out = plogis(-0.5 + 1.5 * stress + 1.0 * treatment),
        p_miss_ss = plogis(-0.5 + 1.2 * age),
        outcome = ifelse(rbinom(n(), 1, p_miss_out) == 1, NA, outcome),
        social_support = ifelse(rbinom(n(), 1, p_miss_ss) == 1, NA, social_support)
    ) |>
    select(-p_miss_out, -p_miss_ss)

# Run MICE
imp <- mice(
    mi_data |> select(-id),
    m = 5, maxit = 20,
    seed = 752, print = FALSE
)

# True model (full data)
true_model <- lm(
    outcome ~ treatment + age + female +
        baseline_severity + social_support,
    data = mi_complete
)

# Complete-case analysis
cc_model <- lm(
    outcome ~ treatment + age + female +
        baseline_severity + social_support,
    data = mi_data
)

# MI: analyze & pool
mi_fit <- with(
    imp,
    lm(outcome ~ treatment + age + female +
        baseline_severity + social_support)
)
mi_pooled <- pool(mi_fit)
```

## Multiple Imputation: The Big Idea

:::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}

Instead of filling in one guess for each missing value, MI creates *m* plausible completed datasets.

**Three steps:**

1.  Impute: Generate *m* completed datasets
2.  Analyze: Fit your model on each one
3.  Pool: Combine with Rubin's Rules

:::


::: {.column width="50%"}

Each imputed dataset is *slightly different*, reflecting our uncertainty about what the missing values could have been.

**Pooled estimate:**

$$\bar{Q} = \frac{1}{m} \sum_{i=1}^{m} \hat{Q}_i$$

**Total variance:**

$$T = \bar{U} + \left(1 + \frac{1}{m}\right) B$$

Where $\bar{U}$ = within-imputation variance and $B$ = between-imputation variance.

:::
::::

## MICE: Chained Equations {.smaller}

**MICE** = **M**ultivariate **I**mputation by **C**hained **E**quations

[MICE website](https://amices.org/mice/){target="_blank"}

Each variable with missing data gets its own imputation model, using all other variables as predictors.

:::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}

**The algorithm:**

1.  Fill in starting values (e.g., random draws from observed)
2.  For each variable with missing data:
    -   Regress it on all other variables (observed cases)
    -   Draw imputed values from the predictive distribution
3.  Repeat step 2 for many iterations (cycling)
4.  Store the final imputed dataset
5.  Repeat *m* times → *m* complete datasets

:::

::: {.column width="50%"}

**Default methods in `mice`:**

| Variable Type    | Method                    |
|------------------|---------------------------|
| Continuous       | Predictive mean matching  |
| Binary (2 lev.)  | Logistic regression       |
| Nominal (>2 lev.)| Multinomial logit         |
| Ordinal          | Proportional odds         |

:::
::::

## A Simulated Clinical Trial {.smaller}

We simulate a randomized trial with 200 participants, two binary predictors, three continuous, and one auxiliary variable (`stress`):

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| eval: false

set.seed(752)
n_mi <- 200

mi_complete <- tibble(
    id = 1:n_mi,
    age = round(rnorm(n_mi, mean = 0, sd = 1), 2),
    female = rbinom(n_mi, 1, 0.55),
    treatment = rbinom(n_mi, 1, 0.5),
    baseline_severity = round(rnorm(n_mi, mean = 0, sd = 1), 2),
    social_support = round(rnorm(n_mi, mean = 0, sd = 1), 2),
    stress = round(rnorm(n_mi, mean = 0, sd = 1), 2),
    outcome = round(
        -0.5 * treatment - 0.3 * age + 0.4 * female +
            0.5 * baseline_severity - 0.3 * social_support +
            0.8 * stress + rnorm(n_mi, 0, 1), 2
    )
)
```

`stress` is an **auxiliary variable**: it affects the outcome but will *not* be included in the analysis model. It will, however, drive missingness and be available to MICE.

**True parameters** (analysis model): $\beta_{\text{trt}} = -0.5$, $\beta_{\text{age}} = -0.3$, $\beta_{\text{female}} = 0.4$, $\beta_{\text{severity}} = 0.5$, $\beta_{\text{support}} = -0.3$

## Making Data Disappear (MAR) {.smaller}

We corrupt the data with MAR missingness. The probability of being missing depends on observed variables:

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| eval: false

mi_data <- mi_complete |>
    mutate(
        # stress (auxiliary) + treatment drive outcome missingness
        p_miss_out = plogis(-0.5 + 1.5 * stress + 1.0 * treatment),
        # Higher age -> more likely to miss social support
        p_miss_ss = plogis(-0.5 + 1.2 * age),
        outcome = ifelse(rbinom(n(), 1, p_miss_out) == 1, NA, outcome),
        social_support = ifelse(rbinom(n(), 1, p_miss_ss) == 1, NA, social_support)
    ) |>
    select(-p_miss_out, -p_miss_ss)
```

This is **MAR** because missingness depends only on **fully observed** variables — `stress` and `treatment` drive missingness in `outcome`, while `age` drives missingness in `social_support`. The key twist: `stress` affects the outcome ($\beta = 0.8$) but is **not in the analysis model**. Complete-case analysis is biased because dropping high-stress treated participants distorts the treatment–outcome relationship (collider bias: treatment $\rightarrow$ R $\leftarrow$ stress). MI recovers because `stress` is included in the imputation model as an auxiliary variable.

## Inspect the Damage {.smaller}

```{r}
#| echo: true

mi_data |>
    summarise(across(everything(), ~ sum(is.na(.x)))) |>
    pivot_longer(everything(), names_to = "Variable", values_to = "N_Missing") |>
    mutate(Pct_Missing = round(N_Missing / nrow(mi_data) * 100, 1)) |>
    filter(N_Missing > 0) |>
    knitr::kable()
```

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 3.5

md.pattern(mi_data |> select(-id), rotate.names = TRUE)
```

Each row is a pattern (1 = observed, 0 = missing). The numbers show how many cases share each pattern.

## Step 1: Run MICE {.smaller}

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| eval: false

library(mice)

imp <- mice(
    mi_data |> select(-id),
    m = 5, # number of imputed datasets
    maxit = 20, # iterations per imputation
    seed = 752,
    print = FALSE
)
```

```{r}
#| echo: true

imp
```

`mice` automatically selects predictive mean matching (pmm) for numeric variables. All fully observed variables serve as predictors in each imputation model.

## Step 2: Check Convergence {.smaller}

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 5

plot(imp)
```

**What to look for**: The *m* colored streams should be freely intermixed with no systematic trend. If streams separate or drift upward/downward check the imputation model.

## Step 3: Inspect Imputed Values {.smaller}

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 4

densityplot(imp)
```

**Blue** = observed data distribution. **Red lines** = imputed distributions (one per imputation). The shapes should be plausible and similar to the observed data, but not necessarily identical.

## Step 4: Analyze Each Imputed Dataset {.smaller}

```{r}
#| echo: true

mi_fit <- with(
    imp,
    lm(outcome ~ treatment + age + female +
        baseline_severity + social_support)
)
```

This fits the same regression model on all `r imp$m` imputed datasets. Each produces slightly different estimates because the imputed values differ.

## Step 5: Pool with Rubin's Rules {.smaller}

```{r}
#| echo: true

mi_pooled <- pool(mi_fit)
summary(mi_pooled, conf.int = TRUE) |>
    mutate(across(where(is.numeric), ~ round(.x, 3))) |>
    select(term, estimate, std.error, `2.5 %`, `97.5 %`, p.value) |>
    knitr::kable()
```

The pooled standard errors incorporate both sampling variability (within) and imputation uncertainty (between).

## Complete-Case vs. MI {.smaller}

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 11
#| fig-height: 5

mi_sum <- summary(mi_pooled, conf.int = TRUE)

plot_data <- bind_rows(
    tibble(
        term = names(coef(true_model)),
        estimate = coef(true_model),
        conf.low = confint(true_model)[, 1],
        conf.high = confint(true_model)[, 2],
        Method = "Full Data (No Missing)"
    ),
    tibble(
        term = names(coef(cc_model)),
        estimate = coef(cc_model),
        conf.low = confint(cc_model)[, 1],
        conf.high = confint(cc_model)[, 2],
        Method = "Complete-Case"
    ),
    tibble(
        term = mi_sum$term,
        estimate = mi_sum$estimate,
        conf.low = mi_sum$`2.5 %`,
        conf.high = mi_sum$`97.5 %`,
        Method = "MI (m = 5)"
    )
) |>
    filter(term != "(Intercept)") |>
    mutate(
        Method = factor(
            Method,
            levels = c("Full Data (No Missing)", "Complete-Case", "MI (m = 5)")
        )
    )

dgp_values <- tibble(
    term = c(
        "treatment", "age", "female",
        "baseline_severity", "social_support"
    ),
    dgp = c(-0.5, -0.3, 0.4, 0.5, -0.3)
)

ggplot(plot_data, aes(x = estimate, y = Method, color = Method)) +
    geom_vline(
        data = dgp_values,
        aes(xintercept = dgp),
        linetype = "dashed", alpha = 0.5
    ) +
    geom_point(size = 3) +
    geom_errorbarh(
        aes(xmin = conf.low, xmax = conf.high),
        height = 0.25
    ) +
    facet_wrap(~term, scales = "free_x", nrow = 1) +
    scale_color_manual(values = c(
        "Full Data (No Missing)" = "#005030",
        "Complete-Case" = "#F47321",
        "MI (m = 5)" = "#003366"
    )) +
    labs(
        x = "Estimate (95% CI)",
        y = "",
        color = "",
        caption = "Dashed line = true DGP value"
    ) +
    theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
    theme(
        legend.position = "bottom",
        strip.text = element_text(face = "bold")
    )
```

- **MI** recovers estimates close to the full-data truth
- **MI standard errors** properly account for imputation uncertainty (between)
- **Complete-case** discards all partially observed rows, losing efficiency

## MI: Practical Guidelines

:::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}

**How many imputations (*m*)?**

-   Old rule of thumb: *m* = 5
-   Other recommendations: ***m* ≥ 20** [@White_2010]
-   Depends on the fraction of missing information

**Include auxiliary variables:**

-   Variables that predict missingness
-   Variables that correlate with the incomplete variable
-   Even if they are not in your analysis model

:::

::: {.column width="50%"}

**Always check:**

-   **Convergence** - trace plots should show no trends
-   **Plausibility** - imputed distributions should be reasonable
-   **Sensitivity** - try different imputation models

**Report in your paper:**

-   Number of imputations (*m*)
-   Imputation method (e.g., PMM, logistic)
-   Variables included in the imputation model
-   Software and version used

:::
::::

::: {.callout-tip}
## The Imputation Model Should Be at Least as General as the Analysis Model
If your analysis includes interactions or nonlinear terms, include them in the imputation model too.
:::

## Other MI Packages in R {.smaller}

Beyond `mice`, several R packages offer alternative approaches to multiple imputation:

| Package | Approach | Best For | Link |
|---------|----------|----------|------|
| **mice** | Chained equations (FCS) | General-purpose, flexible variable-by-variable imputation | [CRAN](https://cran.r-project.org/package=mice) |
| **Amelia** | Joint multivariate normal (EMB algorithm) | Large datasets, continuous/normal data, time-series cross-sectional | [CRAN](https://cran.r-project.org/package=Amelia) |
| **jomo** | Joint modelling with random effects | Multilevel / clustered data, mixed variable types | [CRAN](https://cran.r-project.org/package=jomo) |
| **missForest** | Random forest (single imputation) | Nonlinear relationships, mixed types, no distributional assumptions | [CRAN](https://cran.r-project.org/package=missForest) |
| **miceadds** | Extensions to mice | Multilevel imputation, two-level models, plausible values | [CRAN](https://cran.r-project.org/package=miceadds) |
| **mi** | Bayesian regression | Diagnostics-rich workflow, automatic transformations | [CRAN](https://cran.r-project.org/package=mi) |

**How to choose?**

- **Flat data, mixed types** $\rightarrow$ `mice` (chained equations, most flexible)
- **Mostly continuous, large N** $\rightarrow$ `Amelia` (fast joint model, assumes MVN)
- **Multilevel / clustered** $\rightarrow$ `jomo` or `miceadds` (proper random-effects imputation)
- **Complex nonlinear patterns** $\rightarrow$ `missForest` (tree-based, but single imputation only)


# FIML with lavaan

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| include: false

# --- FIML Setup ---
library(lavaan)

# True population model: 5-item anxiety scale
# Residual variances set to 1 - lambda^2 so that standardized loadings = lambda
pop_model <- "
  anxiety =~ 0.80*item1 + 0.70*item2 + 0.60*item3 + 0.75*item4 + 0.65*item5
  anxiety ~~ 1*anxiety
  item1 ~~ 0.36*item1
  item2 ~~ 0.51*item2
  item3 ~~ 0.64*item3
  item4 ~~ 0.4375*item4
  item5 ~~ 0.5775*item5
"

set.seed(2026)
fiml_complete <- simulateData(pop_model, sample.nobs = 2000)

# Introduce MAR missingness: higher item1 <U+2192> more likely to skip later items
set.seed(303)
fiml_data <- fiml_complete |>
    as_tibble() |>
    mutate(
        item3 = ifelse(
            rbinom(n(), 1, plogis(-2.0 + 0.8 * item1)) == 1, NA, item3
        ),
        item4 = ifelse(
            rbinom(n(), 1, plogis(-1.5 + 0.8 * item1)) == 1, NA, item4
        ),
        item5 = ifelse(
            rbinom(n(), 1, plogis(-1.0 + 0.8 * item1)) == 1, NA, item5
        )
    )

# CFA model
cfa_model <- "
  anxiety =~ item1 + item2 + item3 + item4 + item5
"

# Fit three versions
fit_true <- cfa(cfa_model, data = fiml_complete)
fit_lw <- cfa(cfa_model, data = fiml_data, missing = "listwise")
fit_fiml <- cfa(cfa_model, data = fiml_data, missing = "fiml")
```

## Full Information Maximum Likelihood (FIML)

:::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}

**FIML** estimates model parameters by maximizing the likelihood using all available data, even from incomplete cases.

Unlike MI, FIML does not fill in missing values. Instead, it computes the likelihood for each case based on whatever variables are observed for that case.

:::

::: {.column width="50%"}

**Key properties:**

-   Produces unbiased estimates under MAR
-   Uses all observed information, no cases discarded
-   Handled natively in lavaan or Mplus with a single argument
-   No need to create or manage multiple datasets
-   Equivalent to MI asymptotically (same results, different path)

:::
::::

## A 5-Item Anxiety Scale {.smaller}

We simulate a **one-factor CFA** with 5 items measuring latent anxiety:

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| eval: false

library(lavaan)

pop_model <- "
  anxiety =~ 0.80*item1 + 0.70*item2 + 0.60*item3 + 0.75*item4 + 0.65*item5
  anxiety ~~ 1*anxiety
  item1 ~~ 0.36*item1
  item2 ~~ 0.51*item2
  item3 ~~ 0.64*item3
  item4 ~~ 0.4375*item4
  item5 ~~ 0.5775*item5
"

set.seed(2026)
fiml_complete <- simulateData(pop_model, sample.nobs = 2000)
```

True standardized loadings: $\lambda_1 = .80$, $\lambda_2 = .70$, $\lambda_3 = .60$, $\lambda_4 = .75$, $\lambda_5 = .65$

```{r}
#| echo: true

head(fiml_complete) |>
    mutate(across(everything(), ~ round(.x, 2))) |>
    knitr::kable()
```

## Survey Fatigue Strikes (MAR) {.smaller}

Participants who score higher on item 1 (more anxious) are more likely to skip later items, a realistic survey fatigue pattern:

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| eval: false

fiml_data <- fiml_complete |>
    as_tibble() |>
    mutate(
        # Later items have progressively more missingness
        item3 = ifelse(rbinom(n(), 1, plogis(-2.0 + 0.8 * item1)) == 1, NA, item3),
        item4 = ifelse(rbinom(n(), 1, plogis(-1.5 + 0.8 * item1)) == 1, NA, item4),
        item5 = ifelse(rbinom(n(), 1, plogis(-1.0 + 0.8 * item1)) == 1, NA, item5)
    )
```

This is **MAR**: missingness depends on `item1` (always observed), not on the missing items themselves.

```{r}
#| echo: true

fiml_data |>
    summarise(across(everything(), ~ sum(is.na(.x)))) |>
    pivot_longer(everything(), names_to = "Item", values_to = "N_Missing") |>
    mutate(Pct = round(N_Missing / nrow(fiml_data) * 100, 1)) |>
    filter(N_Missing > 0) |>
    knitr::kable()
```

## The CFA Model in lavaan {.smaller}

The model specification is identical for all three analyses. Only the `missing` argument changes:

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| eval: false

cfa_model <- "
  anxiety =~ item1 + item2 + item3 + item4 + item5
"

# 1. Full data (truth <U+2014> no missing values)
fit_true <- cfa(cfa_model, data = fiml_complete)

# 2. Listwise deletion (default)
fit_lw <- cfa(cfa_model, data = fiml_data, missing = "listwise")

# 3. FIML <U+2014> just add one argument
fit_fiml <- cfa(cfa_model, data = fiml_data, missing = "fiml")
```

::: {.callout-note}
## That's It
The **only** difference is `missing = "fiml"`. lavaan handles everything internally: no imputed datasets, no pooling, no extra steps.
:::

## Listwise vs FIML: Factor Loadings {.smaller}

```{r}
#| echo: false

extract_std <- function(fit) {
    standardizedSolution(fit) |>
        filter(op == "=~") |>
        select(rhs, est.std, se, ci.lower, ci.upper)
}

true_std <- extract_std(fit_true)
lw_std <- extract_std(fit_lw)
fiml_std <- extract_std(fit_fiml)

loading_comparison <- tibble(
    Item = true_std$rhs,
    DGP = c(0.80, 0.70, 0.60, 0.75, 0.65),
    `Full Data` = round(true_std$est.std, 3),
    `Listwise` = round(lw_std$est.std, 3),
    `FIML` = round(fiml_std$est.std, 3),
    `LW (SE)` = round(lw_std$se, 3),
    `FIML (SE)` = round(fiml_std$se, 3)
)

knitr::kable(loading_comparison, align = "lrrrrr")
```

```{r}
#| echo: false

n_true <- lavInspect(fit_true, "nobs")
n_lw <- lavInspect(fit_lw, "nobs")
n_fiml <- lavInspect(fit_fiml, "nobs")
```

| | Full Data | Listwise | FIML |
|---|---|---|---|
| **N used** | `r n_true` | `r n_lw` | `r n_fiml` |

Listwise **discards** every case with any missing item. FIML uses **all `r n_fiml` cases**.

## Listwise vs FIML: Visual Comparison {.smaller}

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 11
#| fig-height: 5

dgp_fiml <- tibble(
    rhs = factor(paste0("item", 1:5), levels = paste0("item", 1:5)),
    dgp = c(0.80, 0.70, 0.60, 0.75, 0.65)
)

plot_fiml_data <- bind_rows(
    extract_std(fit_true) |> mutate(Method = "Full Data (No Missing)"),
    extract_std(fit_lw) |> mutate(Method = "Listwise"),
    extract_std(fit_fiml) |> mutate(Method = "FIML")
) |>
    mutate(
        Method = factor(
            Method,
            levels = c("Full Data (No Missing)", "Listwise", "FIML")
        ),
        rhs = factor(rhs, levels = paste0("item", 1:5))
    )

ggplot(plot_fiml_data, aes(x = est.std, y = Method, color = Method)) +
    geom_vline(
        data = dgp_fiml,
        aes(xintercept = dgp),
        linetype = "dashed", alpha = 0.5
    ) +
    geom_point(size = 3) +
    geom_errorbarh(
        aes(xmin = ci.lower, xmax = ci.upper),
        height = 0.25
    ) +
    facet_wrap(~rhs, scales = "free_x", nrow = 1) +
    scale_color_manual(values = c(
        "Full Data (No Missing)" = "#005030",
        "Listwise" = "#F47321",
        "FIML" = "#003366"
    )) +
    labs(
        x = "Standardized Loading (95% CI)",
        y = "",
        color = "",
        caption = "Dashed line = true population loading"
    ) +
    theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
    theme(
        legend.position = "bottom",
        strip.text = element_text(face = "bold")
    )
```

-   **FIML** recovers loadings close to the truth — especially for items 3–5 where missingness was highest
-   **Listwise** confidence intervals are wider (less efficient) due to reduced sample size

## Model Fit: Listwise vs FIML {.smaller}

```{r}
#| echo: false

fit_idx <- c("chisq", "df", "pvalue", "cfi", "tli", "rmsea", "srmr")

fit_table <- tibble(
    Index = c("<U+03C7><U+00B2>", "df", "p-value", "CFI", "TLI", "RMSEA", "SRMR"),
    `Full Data` = round(fitmeasures(fit_true, fit_idx), 3),
    Listwise = round(fitmeasures(fit_lw, fit_idx), 3),
    FIML = round(fitmeasures(fit_fiml, fit_idx), 3)
)

knitr::kable(fit_table, align = "lrrr")
```

FIML does not improve model fit magically — it provides **more accurate** estimates of the population parameters by using all available information.

```{r}
#| echo: true

# You can inspect the FIML fit just like any lavaan model
summary(fit_fiml, standardized = TRUE, fit.measures = TRUE)
```

## FIML vs MI: When is common to use (not a rule)?

:::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}

**FIML:**

-   Your model is a CFA, SEM, or path model
-   You're already using lavaan / Mplus
-   You want a simple, single-step solution
-   You prefer not to manage multiple datasets

:::

::: {.column width="50%"}

**MI:**

-   Your analysis is not SEM-based (e.g., regression, ANOVA, mixed models)
-   You need to use software that doesn't support FIML
-   You want to include many auxiliary variables flexibly
-   You need to do sensitivity analyses with different imputation models

:::
::::

. . .

::: {.callout-important}
Both MI and FIML assume MAR. If you suspect MNAR, you need sensitivity analysis, neither method alone can save you.
:::

## Wrapping Up: Your Complete Toolkit

| Method               | When to Use                           | Assumption | Bias? |
|----------------------|---------------------------------------|------------|-------|
| **Complete-case**    | Quick look, MCAR only                 | MCAR       | No (under MCAR) |
| **MI (MICE)**        | Any model, any software               | MAR        | No (under MAR)   |
| **FIML**    | CFA / SEM models                      | MAR        | No (under MAR)   |
| **Sensitivity**      | When MNAR is suspected                | MNAR       | Depends          |

**Your workflow:**

1.  **Diagnose** Why is data missing? (MCAR / MAR / MNAR)
2.  **Choose** Pick the right tool for your model and mechanism
3.  **Check** Convergence, plausibility, sensitivity
4.  **Report** Be transparent about what you did and why
